result.question: Survey the functionality and design approaches implemented by existing Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol SDKs (official a2a-python, a2a-js, a2a-java, a2a-go, a2a-dotnet, plus notable community SDKs and framework integrations like Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework/Semantic Kernel, LangGraph, BeeAI). For each: supported transports (JSON-RPC, gRPC, HTTP+JSON/REST), spec version conformance (0.3 / 1.0), agent card features (signing, extended card, discovery), task store and queue abstractions (in-memory, DB, Redis), push notifications, streaming/resubscribe, auth/security schemes, client features (factory, transport negotiation, interceptors), server hosting integration, telemetry/OpenTelemetry, testing/TCK support, packaging. Goal: inform the design of a .NET A2A SDK — highlight patterns worth copying and gaps.
result.summary: The A2A project lists six official SDKs under the a2aproject GitHub org: Python, Go, Java, JavaScript, C#/.NET and Rust. a2a-dotnet is the upstream .NET reference to compare against. The SDKs verified here (a2a-js 1.0.0 GA, a2a-go v2, a2a-java 1.0.0.Beta1, a2a-python 1.0) now target spec v1.0. All support JSON-RPC, HTTP+JSON/REST and gRPC as equal transports, and a2a-js and a2a-go also offer explicit v0.3 compatibility paths. The patterns most worth copying come mainly from Python and Java. Python has pluggable TaskStore and PushNotificationConfigStore interfaces with in-memory and SQL versions, data scoped per owner, best-effort push delivery with a URL validator, a ClientFactory that chooses a transport from the agent card and lets you register custom transports, and a signature-verifier hook when fetching the card. Java ships each transport and each persistence/clustering add-on (JPA stores, a replicated queue for resubscribe across instances) as a separate module managed by a BOM. The verified evidence says nothing about Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph or BeeAI, and it covers telemetry, TCK and a2a-dotnet's own features only briefly.

findings.claim: There are six official A2A SDKs, all under the a2aproject GitHub org: a2a-python, a2a-go, a2a-java, a2a-js, a2a-dotnet and a2a-rs. a2a-dotnet is the only official .NET SDK, so it is the natural baseline for a new .NET SDK.
findings.evidence: The official SDK table on the protocol docs site lists exactly these six repos (claims 0, 1). Calling a2a-dotnet the comparison baseline is an inference.

findings.claim: The main SDKs have moved to spec v1.0 and give v0.3 a separate migration path. a2a-js 1.0.0 is GA and makes v0.3 support opt-in. a2a-go v2 exports a2a.Version and has an a2acompat/a2av0 package with 0.3 agent card types. a2a-java 1.0.0.Beta1 is aligned with the final 1.0.0 spec. a2a-python has v1.0 API docs.
findings.evidence: Claims 2, 5, 6, 13. In a2a-go, v0.3 compatibility may cover only the agent card types, not the full protocol. Pattern to copy: v1.0 as the default, with v0.3 support in a separate package you choose to add.

findings.claim: All three transports (JSON-RPC, HTTP+JSON/REST, gRPC) are now treated as equal in JS, Go and Java. Go has one transport-neutral handler (a2asrv.NewHandler) wrapped by a2agrpc.NewHandler, a2asrv.NewRESTHandler and a2asrv.NewJSONRPCHandler. Java turns on each transport by adding its own artifact (-reference-jsonrpc/-grpc/-rest) and manages versions with a2a-java-sdk-bom.
findings.evidence: Claims 3, 4, 7, 8. Pattern for .NET: one core request handler with thin adapters per transport, shipped as separate NuGet packages (for example Server.Grpc, Server.Rest), with a meta-package or shared version props acting like a BOM.

findings.claim: In a2a-python, task storage is a pluggable abstract TaskStore with save/get/delete/list(ListTasksRequest). It ships InMemoryTaskStore (use_copying=True deep-copies by default) and a SQLAlchemy DatabaseTaskStore (AsyncEngine, create_table flag, configurable table_name, model-conversion hooks).
findings.evidence: Claims 10, 13. Every method also takes a ServerCallContext. Patterns worth copying: deep-copy in memory so callers cannot change stored tasks, and an optional schema auto-create.

findings.claim: a2a-python scopes data by owner. Every store takes an owner_resolver (default resolve_user_scope, Callable[[ServerCallContext], str]). The push config store separates get_info, which returns only the caller's configs, from get_info_for_dispatch, which reads across owners for the dispatch loop. The default dispatch fallback uses an empty context and returns nothing, so custom stores must override it.
findings.evidence: Claims 11, 14. This is an important multi-tenant design point: build owner isolation into the store contract, and give dispatch its own explicit cross-owner read path. The Python fallback trap is a gap to avoid; make it abstract or required in .NET.

findings.claim: In a2a-python, push notifications are split into a PushNotificationConfigStore (in-memory, or SQLAlchemy with an optional Fernet encryption_key for configs at rest) and a PushNotificationSender. BasePushNotificationSender uses an httpx AsyncClient plus the config store, accepts an optional async push_url_validator (an SSRF guard hook), and is best-effort: failures are logged and never affect the task lifecycle or event stream.
findings.evidence: Claims 11, 12, 15. Patterns to copy: encrypt stored push configs (which can contain webhook credentials), validate push URLs through a pluggable hook, and keep delivery failures out of the task flow. The docs do not mention retries or a durable outbox, which is a possible gap.

findings.claim: a2a-java offers persistence and clustering as optional Extras modules that replace the in-memory defaults. JpaDatabaseTaskStore (a2a-java-extras-task-store-database-jpa) and JpaDatabasePushNotificationConfigStore take over through CDI @Alternative/@Priority when on the classpath. ReplicatedQueueManager wraps InMemoryQueueManager and uses a pluggable ReplicationStrategy (reference: MicroProfile Reactive Messaging, tested with Kafka) to push EventQueue events and queue create/close notices to other nodes, so streaming and resubscribe work on any instance.
findings.evidence: Claims 9, 16, 17. Resubscribe across instances also needs a shared, persistent TaskStore. Extras also include OpenTelemetry, multitenancy and other HTTP clients. Pattern for .NET: an IQueueManager abstraction plus a replication strategy (for example Redis pub/sub or Kafka), and an EF Core task store, each in its own package registered through DI.

findings.claim: a2a-python's client uses a ClientFactory built from a ClientConfig. create(card, interceptors) negotiates a transport by matching the client config against the agent card's interfaces and raises ValueError when nothing matches. register(label, generator) adds custom transports, where the generator is (AgentCard, url, ClientConfig) -> ClientTransport. Interceptors (ClientCallInterceptor) are passed in when the client is created.
findings.evidence: Claims 18, 19, 21, 22. In 0.3.x the producer also took an interceptors list; in v1.0 it no longer does. Pattern: a transport registry keyed by protocol label, an ordered client preference list, and a clear error when nothing matches.

findings.claim: In a2a-python, client discovery is create_from_url. It fetches <url>/.well-known/agent-card.json by default using the factory's httpx client, relative_card_path overrides the path, and resolver_http_kwargs is passed to the HTTP call. It accepts an optional signature_verifier: Callable[[AgentCard], None] for checking signed cards. The SDK provides the hook; you supply the verification logic.
findings.evidence: Claims 20, 23. Gap to fill in .NET: ship a built-in JWS verifier (a JWKS-backed default) on top of the hook, not just the hook.

findings.claim: In a2a-java, security is handed to the host framework. The Quarkus reference servers already mark protected JSON-RPC, gRPC and REST endpoints with @Authenticated. Securing a server mostly means adding quarkus-oidc (Keycloak via Dev Services) and declaring an OAuth2 client-credentials scheme in the agent card's securitySchemes and security fields.
findings.evidence: Claim 24. Single blog source, but the verifier checked current a2a-java master and the annotations are still on all three transports, with auth tests for each. The blog targets protocol 0.3, where field names may differ. ASP.NET Core equivalent: RequireAuthorization() on mapped endpoints, plus card scheme declarations built from the configured auth.

result.caveats: The verified claims cover only the official Python, Go, Java and JS SDKs. Framework integrations (Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework/Semantic Kernel, LangGraph, BeeAI), community SDKs, a2a-rs and a2a-dotnet's own features are not covered, so these findings cannot support a direct comparison with a2a-dotnet. Telemetry (beyond Java listing an OpenTelemetry extra), TCK support, server-side signing of agent cards, the extended card, and how resubscribe is implemented outside Java were not verified. Several findings rest on maintainer blog posts (Quarkus) rather than code. a2a-java 1.0.0.Beta1 is pre-GA, and its JPA and replication details come from 0.3.x posts that may have changed in 1.0. Python details come from API docs, not source code, and say nothing about retries or encryption specifics beyond the Fernet mention. The SDKs are changing fast (2025-2026 releases), so version details may age quickly.
openQuestions: What does a2a-dotnet support today (transports, v1.0 conformance, stores, push, card signing, ASP.NET Core integration), and where does it fall short of the Python and Java patterns above?
Which SDKs pass the official A2A TCK for v1.0, and how do they wire TCK runs into CI?
How do the SDKs handle OpenTelemetry (span names, propagation across streaming and push) and server-side agent card signing (JWS/JWKS)?
Do Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph and BeeAI build on the official SDKs or reimplement the protocol, and which hosting patterns do they add?
